title: What does APRA CPS 234 require for information security training?
description: CPS 234 sets no course, but its capability, roles and policy duties drive security awareness training. What APRA expects and how to evidence it.
shortAnswer: Prudential Standard CPS 234 Information Security, made by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA), does not mandate a specific training course. It requires regulated entities to define information security roles, maintain an information security capability that includes skills, and give direction on security responsibilities to all staff, contractors and third parties. APRA's guide CPG 234 describes the training and awareness program it expects, including tracking training and testing understanding on commencement and periodically.
keyTakeaways: CPS 234 has applied since July 1, 2019 to ADIs, general and life insurers, private health insurers and RSE licensees.
The standard defines information security capability as "the totality of resources, skills and controls", so staff skills are part of what must be maintained.

Paragraph 19 requires the policy framework to give direction on the responsibilities of all parties, which footnote 8 extends to all staff, contractors, consultants, related parties, third parties and customers.
CPG 234 Attachment B sets out APRA's expected training and awareness content and says sound practice tracks training and tests understanding.
Testing and assurance must be done by appropriately skilled people, and material incidents must be notified to APRA within 72 hours.
appliesTo: Authorised deposit-taking institutions (ADIs) and authorised banking NOHCs
General insurers, life companies and private health insurers
RSE licensees in respect of their business operations
Boards, senior management, staff and contractors of these entities

sections.heading: Does CPS 234 require security awareness training?

blocks.text: CPS 234 does not use the word training, but several of its requirements cannot be met without it. The standard, published in full on APRA's [CPS 234 page](https://www.apra.gov.au/standards/cps-234), makes the Board ultimately responsible for information security (paragraph 13) and requires the entity to clearly define the information security roles and responsibilities of the Board, senior management, governing bodies and individuals (paragraph 14).

Paragraph 15 requires an information security capability commensurate with the size and extent of threats, and paragraph 17 requires it to be actively maintained as vulnerabilities and threats change. The standard defines that capability as "the totality of resources, skills and controls which provide the ability and capacity to maintain information security". Paragraph 19 then requires the policy framework to "provide direction on the responsibilities of all parties who have an obligation to maintain information security", and footnote 8 says parties include "all other staff, contractors, consultants, related parties, third parties and customers".

Read together, these provisions mean an entity must be able to show that people with security responsibilities know what they are and have the skills to carry them out. Training and awareness is the usual way to show it, and it is the lens APRA uses in [CPG 234](https://www.apra.gov.au/practice-guides/cpg-234).

sections.heading: What training content does APRA expect?

blocks.text: APRA's expected content is set out in Attachment B of CPG 234, the prudential practice guide issued in June 2019. APRA says an entity "could benefit from developing a training and information security awareness program" covering staff, contractors and third parties, with material for the Board and governing bodies, and that "sound practice would involve tracking training undertaken and testing the understanding of relevant information security policies, both on commencement and periodically".
CPG 234 lists common areas for regular user education:

items: personal versus corporate use of information assets
email, internet (including social networking) and malware protection
physical protection, remote computing and mobile devices
common attack techniques aimed at personnel and facilities, such as social engineering and tailgating
access controls, passwords and other authentication requirements
responsibilities for end user developed or configured software, including spreadsheets and databases
expectations where bring your own device is allowed
reporting information security incidents and concerns

blocks.text: CPG 234 also says all users would typically be required to periodically sign off on relevant security policies as part of their employment or contractual terms. A [policy attestation](/glossary/policy-attestation) records that sign off, but it is not evidence of understanding on its own.

sections.heading: Which roles need more than general awareness?

blocks.text: Board members, incident responders, testers and internal auditors need role specific capability, because CPS 234 places specific duties on each. The table below is an original mapping of CPS 234 paragraphs to learning outcomes and evidence, for illustration.

sections.heading: How should entities measure security awareness?

blocks.text: Measure coverage, understanding and behavior, not just completion. CPG 234's list of common Board and management metrics includes "Awareness exercises (coverage %, count)" and "Staff responding to phishing tests (% of total staff)", and its list of education reporting items includes the results of training and awareness sessions.

Useful measures for an [audit trail](/glossary/audit-trail) include the proportion of in-scope staff and contractors trained within a set period of starting, pass rates on policy knowledge checks, phishing simulation outcomes over time, and the number and quality of staff-reported incidents. Where a third party manages information assets, CPS 234 paragraphs 16 and 22 require the entity to assess that party's capability and control design, which can include how the provider trains its own staff. The guide on [showing a regulator that training works](/guides/how-to-evidence-training-effectiveness-to-a-regulator) covers how to present this evidence.

sections.heading: How does CPS 234 connect to CPS 230 and incident notification?

blocks.text: CPS 230 requires entities to meet CPS 234 as part of managing technology risk, so security capability is also an operational resilience issue. Paragraph 24 of the version of CPS 230 in force from July 1, 2026 says an entity "must meet the requirements for information security" in CPS 234; see [CPS 230 and staff capability](/regulations/apra-cps-230-operational-risk-training).

Staff also need to know the notification clocks that their escalations feed. Under CPS 234 an entity must notify APRA no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a material information security incident (paragraph 35), and no later than 10 business days after becoming aware of a material control weakness it does not expect to remediate in a timely manner (paragraph 36). Late internal reporting shortens the time available, so incident reporting belongs in every user's training. This summary reflects the standard as at September 2026.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry maps CPS 234 duties, CPG 234 topics and an entity's own security policies into one framework, then links each role to the concepts it must understand and the assessment that proves it. When a policy changes, the affected roles and questions are identified from the framework, and the evidence shows which policy version each person was assessed on.

faqs.q: Is annual security awareness training mandatory under CPS 234?
faqs.a: CPS 234 does not set a frequency. CPG 234 describes sound practice as tracking training and testing understanding on commencement and periodically. Many entities choose an annual cycle with more frequent phishing simulations, but the interval should be justified by the threat environment and the entity's own risk assessment.

faqs.q: Do contractors and third parties need training?
faqs.a: The policy framework must give direction to all parties with an obligation to maintain information security, which footnote 8 of CPS 234 extends to contractors, consultants, related parties and third parties. CPG 234 includes contractors and third parties in the expected training and awareness program.

faqs.q: Does the Board need security training?
faqs.a: The Board is ultimately responsible for information security under paragraph 13 of CPS 234, and CPG 234 says awareness material should help the Board and governing bodies execute their duties. Directors need enough understanding to interpret security reporting and challenge management.

No. CPG 234 is guidance that sets out APRA's view of sound practice and how it interprets CPS 234. The standard itself is binding. APRA uses the guide in supervision, so departing from it should be a documented, reasoned decision.
